beats.trigger: Security
beats.got: nothing new, just a heading

beats.trigger: It is important to involve the right stakeholders early, to follow best practices, and to keep iterating as the landscape changes.
beats.got: nothing new. This is the 2017 slide.

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: Homework with three links, and I'm not reading them tonight.

beats.trigger: **Distinguish** compliant, violating and "I can't tell" for each rule
beats.got: The checks allow an 'I can't tell' answer. That is more honest than I expected.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I'm asked to start with my own doubts, which is fine.

beats.trigger: A tool call is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: The agent's text becomes actions through plain tool calls. I can ask it three questions myself and check.

beats.trigger: Leading companies are investing in enablement programmes, champions networks and training, and the ones that start early will be best placed.
beats.got: nothing new. A claim about the future with no evidence. Champions networks were also in the OKR deck.

beats.trigger: Classical software security is a risk-based practice, and the software it protects is deterministic: same input, same output.
beats.got: Old security assumed the software behaves the same every time. I knew that.

beats.trigger: The dangerous move is getting your agent to *decide* to do something harmful with access it has, through well-formed English in a document it reads.
beats.got: An ordinary document can steer the agent into harm. That is a real difference from normal software, and a concrete one.

beats.trigger: Remember that success with AI is everyone's responsibility.
beats.got: nothing new. Sponsorship and follow-up, as in every programme.

beats.trigger: This is a rapidly evolving area, and organisations of every size are working out how best to approach it.
beats.got: nothing new. It's the same paragraph a second time.

beats.trigger: Scope it down far enough and the system is safe and useless.
beats.got: Safe and useful pull against each other, and someone has to sign for where the line sits. That is candid.

beats.trigger: Expect it to cost you a feature.
beats.got: The cheapest security is not connecting things, and it costs you a feature. It is rare for a course to say that.

beats.trigger: the ones that start early will be best placed.
beats.got: nothing new. Third time this slide has shown up.

beats.trigger: a skill is a reusable check you run again instead of re-prompting from memory.
beats.got: A skill is a saved, repeatable check instead of retyping prompts. Fine, practical.

beats.trigger: Read the first few rows: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: The agent checks my policies against my system and says which rules it can't judge. I can test that myself.

beats.trigger: Push back on anything that sounds like a generic GDPR brochure.
beats.got: My own concerns go in as rules, so the check ends up specific to our company and not generic.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: Policy plus agent-risk checks in one skill. Twenty-two minutes of Q&A.

beats.trigger: *"You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."*
beats.got: I can hand decisions back to the agent when I don't know the answer.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/agent-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: Procedure for saving the file. I'd leave that to my team.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: This doesn't replace our security people. It sits on top of what they do. That is the right answer.

beats.trigger: Clear communication, strong sponsorship and regular follow-up remain the foundation
beats.got: nothing new. I stopped reading these a while ago.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: Check that the skill shows up in the list.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: It might show me gaps in my own assumptions, and I can verify that by reading the report rows.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: A ranked list of risks in my own system. The line about feelings is a little coach-like, though.

beats.trigger: It is important to involve the right stakeholders early, to follow best practices
beats.got: nothing new. The paragraph is back again.

beats.trigger: The narrow question the expert can answer is sitting in the report. Walk in with that.
beats.got: When the agent can't decide, I take the evidence to legal or security with a narrow question. That is how I'd do it anyway.

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent.
beats.got: One risk handled is a demo, not a production system. True, though 'you must do the work' is a bit nagging.

beats.trigger: Industry analysts expect agent adoption to accelerate significantly over the coming years.
beats.got: nothing new. Analysts again, with no source.

beats.trigger: "That residual is too vague, name the file or behaviour."
beats.got: The agent writes rules for future sessions from the audit, and I push back where it's vague. That is checkable.

beats.trigger: A skill is not a deployed service and does not settle ownership.
beats.got: Skills can be shared, but that doesn't solve who owns them. Candid about the limit.

beats.trigger: agents are simply one more area where those principles apply.
beats.got: nothing new. This is the tenth interruption of this kind.

beats.trigger: Your call.
beats.got: Homework: write two sentences about two cases. Not tonight.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two real failures to read. Real cases beat slides, so I might read them.

take_homes: Agents can be steered by text in documents they read, so what you let them read and change is the real security decision.
Don't connect what you don't need. It costs a feature but removes the risk.
When the check says 'I can't tell', take that exact question to legal or security.

monday.move: Ask whoever owns our first pilot what the agent can read and what it can change, and write the answer down on one page.
monday.who: my pilot owner and our security lead
monday.stop_condition: if nobody can answer within a week, the pilot gets no further access
monday.blocker: My calendar is full of the last programme's steering groups. I also won't run the exercises myself.

misconception.why: A text document steering the agent into harm is actually new and not something we had with agile or OKRs. I'm still not sure wait-and-see is wrong, but the door-you-don't-open slide shows the risk is manageable now. I'd also be more convinced if the course didn't keep repeating the same generic paragraphs.

one_line: The security core is concrete and honest about limits, but about ten slides in between are the same generic paragraph, and without them it would be a good module.
